amc12-2021-12a-02.title: Square carefully
amc12-2021-12a-02.body:
A square root is never negative, so we need $a+b\ge0$. When $a+b\ge0$, the equation is equivalent to its square: $a^2+b^2=a^2+2ab+b^2$, i.e. $ab=0$. So it holds exactly when $ab=0$ and $a+b\ge0$.

**Answer: (D)**

amc12-2021-12a-02.title: Test the options
amc12-2021-12a-02.body:
$a=b=0$ works, so (A) is false. $a=1,b=1$: $\sqrt2\ne2$, so (C) and (E) are false. $a=-1,b=0$: $\sqrt1=1\ne-1$, so (B) is false even though $ab=0$. That leaves (D), which the algebra confirms.

**Answer: (D)**

amc12-2021-12a-06.title: Equations
amc12-2021-12a-06.body:
Let there be $r$ red cards and $n$ cards in all: $n=3r$ and $n+4=4r$. Subtracting, $r=4$, so $n=12$.

**Answer: (C) $12$**

amc12-2021-12a-06.title: Ratios
amc12-2021-12a-06.body:
Originally red : black $=1:2$; afterwards $1:3$. The red count didn't change, and the black count went up by $4$, which is one more "red's worth". So there are $4$ red and $8$ black cards: $12$ in total.

**Answer: (C) $12$**

amc12-2021-12a-08.title: Parities repeat
amc12-2021-12a-08.body:
Work mod $2$ ($E=0$, $O=1$):
$$D_0,\dots,D_9:\ 0,0,1,1,1,0,1,0,0,1.$$
$D_7,D_8,D_9=0,0,1$ equals $D_0,D_1,D_2$, and each term depends only on the previous three, so the parities repeat with period $7$.

$2021=7\cdot288+5$, so $(D_{2021},D_{2022},D_{2023})$ has the parities of $(D_5,D_6,D_7)=(0,1,0)$: $(E,O,E)$.

**Answer: (C) $(E,O,E)$**

amc12-2021-12a-11.title: Unfold the reflections
amc12-2021-12a-11.body:
Reflecting the target across the $x$-axis and then across the $y$-axis turns the bouncing path into a straight segment of the same length, from $(3,5)$ to $(-7,-5)$. Its length is $\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt2$.

**Answer: (C) $10\sqrt2$**

amc12-2021-12a-11.title: Find the bounce points
amc12-2021-12a-11.body:
The straight line from $(3,5)$ to $(-7,-5)$ has slope $1$: $y=x+2$. It meets the $y$-axis at $(0,2)$. After the bounce the beam goes along slope $-1$: $y=2-x$, reaching the $x$-axis at $(2,0)$, then along slope $1$ to $(7,5)$. Lengths: $3\sqrt2+2\sqrt2+5\sqrt2=10\sqrt2$.

**Answer: (C) $10\sqrt2$**

amc12-2021-12a-13.title: Polar form
amc12-2021-12a-13.body:
All five numbers have modulus $2$, so $z^5=32(\cos5\theta+i\sin5\theta)$ and we compare $\cos5\theta$:
- $-2$: $\theta=180^\circ$, $5\theta=900^\circ\equiv180^\circ$: $\cos=-1$.
- $-\sqrt3+i$: $\theta=150^\circ$, $5\theta=750^\circ\equiv30^\circ$: $\cos=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
- $-\sqrt2+\sqrt2i$: $\theta=135^\circ$, $5\theta=675^\circ\equiv315^\circ$: $\cos=\frac{\sqrt2}2$.
- $-1+\sqrt3i$: $\theta=120^\circ$, $5\theta=600^\circ\equiv240^\circ$: $\cos=-\frac12$.
- $2i$: $\theta=90^\circ$, $5\theta\equiv90^\circ$: $\cos=0$.

The largest is $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ (real part $16\sqrt3$).

**Answer: (B) $-\sqrt3+i$**

amc12-2021-12a-14.title: Simplify each term
amc12-2021-12a-14.body:
$\log_{5^k}3^{k^2}=\frac{k^2\ln3}{k\ln5}=k\log_53$, so the first sum is $(1+\dots+20)\log_53=210\log_53$.

$\log_{9^k}25^k=\frac{k\ln25}{k\ln9}=\frac{2\ln5}{2\ln3}=\log_35$, so the second sum is $100\log_35$.

Since $\log_53\cdot\log_35=1$, the product is $210\cdot100=21{,}000$.

**Answer: (E) $21{,}000$**

amc12-2021-12a-15.title: Choose the basses left out
amc12-2021-12a-15.body:
Instead of choosing $b$ basses, choose the $8-b$ basses who are *not* in the group. A group corresponds to a set of $t$ tenors plus $8-b$ excluded basses, i.e. a subset of the $14$ singers of size $t+8-b$. The condition $4\mid t-b$ is the same as $4\mid t+8-b$.

So the number of groups (allowing the empty one) is the number of subsets of $14$ people with size a multiple of $4$:
$$\binom{14}0+\binom{14}4+\binom{14}8+\binom{14}{12}=1+1001+3003+91=4096.$$
Removing the empty group, $N=4095$, and $N\bmod100=95$.

**Answer: (D) $95$**

amc12-2021-12a-15.title: Direct casework
amc12-2021-12a-15.body:
Sum $\binom6t\binom8b$ over $t\equiv b\pmod4$:
- $t-b=0$: $\sum_t\binom6t\binom8t=\sum_t\binom6t\binom8{8-t}=\binom{14}{8}=3003$ (Vandermonde).
- $t-b=4$: $\binom64\binom80+\binom65\binom81+\binom66\binom82=15+48+28=91$.
- $t-b=-4$: $\binom60\binom84+\binom61\binom85+\binom62\binom86+\binom63\binom87+\binom64\binom88=70+336+420+160+15=1001$.
- $t-b=-8$: $\binom60\binom88=1$.

Total $3003+91+1001+1=4096$, including the empty group. So $N=4095$.

**Answer: (D) $95$**

amc12-2021-12a-19.title: Turn cosine into sine
amc12-2021-12a-19.body:
Write the right side as $\sin\left(\frac\pi2-\frac\pi2\sin x\right)$. For $x\in[0,\pi]$, $\frac\pi2\cos x\in[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]$ and $\frac\pi2-\frac\pi2\sin x\in[0,\frac\pi2]$. Sine is one-to-one on $[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]$, so the equation is equivalent to
$$\frac\pi2\cos x=\frac\pi2-\frac\pi2\sin x\iff\sin x+\cos x=1.$$
Then $\sqrt2\sin(x+\frac\pi4)=1$, so $x+\frac\pi4\in\{\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4\}$, i.e. $x=0$ or $x=\frac\pi2$. Two solutions.

**Answer: (C) $2$**

amc12-2021-12a-19.title: Square the simplified equation
amc12-2021-12a-19.body:
From $\sin x+\cos x=1$, squaring gives $2\sin x\cos x=0$, so $\sin x=0$ or $\cos x=0$: candidates $x=0,\frac\pi2,\pi$. Checking in $\sin x+\cos x=1$: $x=0$ ✓, $x=\frac\pi2$ ✓, $x=\pi$ gives $-1$ ✗. Directly in the original: $x=0$: $\sin\frac\pi2=1=\cos0$ ✓; $x=\frac\pi2$: $\sin0=0=\cos\frac\pi2$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) $2$**

amc12-2021-12a-20.title: Coordinates
amc12-2021-12a-20.body:
Let $FV=p$, $V=(0,0)$, $F=(0,p)$; the parabola is $x^2=4py$ with directrix $y=-p$. For $A=(x,y)$ on it, $AF$ equals the distance to the directrix: $y+p=20$, so $y=20-p$ and $x^2=4p(20-p)$.

Then $AV^2=x^2+y^2=4p(20-p)+(20-p)^2=(20-p)(20+3p)=441$, i.e.
$$3p^2-40p+41=0.$$
Its discriminant $1600-492>0$, both roots are positive and less than $20$ (so $y>0$), and they sum to $\frac{40}3$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{40}3$**

amc12-2021-12a-21.title: Fit an axis-parallel ellipse
amc12-2021-12a-21.body:
The roots are $1$, $-1\pm\sqrt3i$, $-2\pm\sqrt2i$: points $(1,0)$, $(-1,\pm\sqrt3)$, $(-2,\pm\sqrt2)$. The point set is symmetric about the $x$-axis and the ellipse is unique, so it is symmetric too: $\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$. Write $A=\frac1{a^2}$, $B=\frac1{b^2}$:
$$(1-h)^2A=1,\qquad(1+h)^2A+3B=1,\qquad(2+h)^2A+2B=1.$$
Eliminate $B$ ($3\times$ third $-\ 2\times$ second): $A\left[3(2+h)^2-2(1+h)^2\right]=1=A(1-h)^2$, so
$$10+8h+h^2=1-2h+h^2\implies h=-\tfrac9{10}.$$
Then $a^2=(1-h)^2=\frac{361}{100}$ and $3B=1-\frac{(1/10)^2}{361/100}=\frac{360}{361}$, so $b^2=\frac{361}{120}$.

Since $a^2>b^2$, the major axis is horizontal and $e^2=1-\frac{b^2}{a^2}=1-\frac{100}{120}=\frac16$. So $m+n=7$.

**Answer: (A) $7$**

amc12-2021-12a-22.title: Vieta with trig identities
amc12-2021-12a-22.body:
Let $c_k=\cos\frac{2k\pi}7$ for $k=1,2,3$; note $\cos\frac{8\pi}7=c_3$, $\cos\frac{10\pi}7=c_2$, $\cos\frac{12\pi}{7}=c_1$.

**Sum.** The real parts of the $7$th roots of unity add to $0$: $1+2(c_1+c_2+c_3)=0$, so $c_1+c_2+c_3=-\frac12$ and $a=\frac12$.

**Pairwise products.** Using $2\cos u\cos v=\cos(u-v)+\cos(u+v)$: $2c_1c_2=c_1+c_3$, $2c_1c_3=c_2+c_3$ (as $\cos\frac{8\pi}7=c_3$), $2c_2c_3=c_1+c_2$ (as $\cos\frac{10\pi}7=c_2$). Adding, $c_1c_2+c_1c_3+c_2c_3=c_1+c_2+c_3=-\frac12$, so $b=-\frac12$.

**Product.** With $\theta=\frac{2\pi}7$, $8\sin\theta\cos\theta\cos2\theta\cos4\theta=\sin8\theta=\sin\theta$ (since $8\theta=2\pi+\theta$). So $\cos\theta\cos2\theta\cos4\theta=\frac18$, and $\cos4\theta=\cos\frac{8\pi}7=c_3$. Thus $c_1c_2c_3=\frac18$ and $c=-\frac18$.

$abc=\frac12\cdot\left(-\frac12\right)\cdot\left(-\frac18\right)=\frac1{32}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac1{32}$**

amc12-2021-12a-24.title: Radical axis in coordinates
amc12-2021-12a-24.body:
$P,Q,R$ lie on $\Omega$, so by the extended law of sines its radius is $\frac{QR}{2\sin60^\circ}=3$. Put the center of $\Gamma$ at the origin ($x^2+y^2=49$, $y\ge0$), $P=(p,0)$ and the center of $\Omega$ at $O'=(p,3)$, so $\Omega$ is $x^2+y^2-2px-6y+p^2=0$.

Subtracting the two circle equations, line $QR$ is $2px+6y=p^2+49$.

The chord $QR=3\sqrt3$ of $\Omega$ is at distance $\sqrt{9-\frac{27}4}=\frac32$ from $O'$:
$$\frac{|2p^2+18-p^2-49|}{\sqrt{4p^2+36}}=\frac32\iff (p^2-31)^2=9p^2+81\iff p^4-71p^2+880=0,$$
so $p^2=16$ or $55$. Since $P$ is on the diameter, $p^2<49$, so $p=\pm4$; take $p=4$. Line $QR$: $8x+6y=65$.

The distance from $P=(4,0)$ to $QR$ is $\frac{|32-65|}{10}=\frac{33}{10}$. ($P$ and $O'$ are on the same side of $QR$, so $P$ is on the major arc of $\Omega$, consistent with $\angle QPR=60^\circ$ rather than $120^\circ$.)

Area $=\frac12\cdot3\sqrt3\cdot\frac{33}{10}=\frac{99\sqrt3}{20}$, so $a+b+c=99+3+20=122$.

**Answer: (D) $122$**

amc12-2021-12a-25.title: Optimize one prime at a time
amc12-2021-12a-25.body:
If $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ then $f(n)=\prod\frac{e_i+1}{p_i^{e_i/3}}$, so we can choose each exponent separately to maximize $g_p(e)=\frac{e+1}{p^{e/3}}$ (with $g_p(0)=1$).

- $p=2$: $g=1,\ \frac{2}{2^{1/3}}\approx1.59,\ \frac{3}{2^{2/3}}\approx1.89,\ \frac42=2,\ \frac{5}{2^{4/3}}\approx1.98$, then decreasing. Best $e=3$.
- $p=3$: $\frac{2}{3^{1/3}}\approx1.39,\ \frac{3}{3^{2/3}}\approx1.44,\ \frac43\approx1.33$. Best $e=2$.
- $p=5$: $\frac2{5^{1/3}}\approx1.17$ vs. $\frac{3}{5^{2/3}}\approx1.03$. Best $e=1$.
- $p=7$: $\frac{2}{7^{1/3}}\approx1.05>1$ (since $8>7$), and $\frac3{7^{2/3}}<1$. Best $e=1$.
- $p\ge11$: $\frac{2}{p^{1/3}}<1$ (since $p>8$), and higher powers are worse. Best $e=0$.

So $N=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7=2520$, whose digit sum is $9$.

**Answer: (E) $9$**
